Visuospatial function preserved; naming low average. 4. Elevated informant-rated frontal behaviour (FBI 30/72). The profile is executive and social-cognitive predominant with relative sparing of visuospatial function, consistent with a frontal-network syndrome; the memory deficit is not specific and does not exclude an Alzheimer-type process.

output.impression: 1. Heterozygous pathogenic C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion (more than 400 repeats). 2. No pathogenic variant in GRN or MAPT. The C9orf72 expansion is associated with frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with age-dependent, incomplete penetrance; each child of a carrier has a 50% chance of inheriting it. Post-test genetic counselling is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).

Explain why Alzheimer disease is less likely despite the impaired free recall (behaviour-led onset, frontal-predominant atrophy with preserved posterior cortex, partial benefit from recognition), and that an amyloid or CSF AD biomarker study can settle the question.
Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, given her brother's ALS and her mother's mid-life psychiatric illness, and discuss what a result would mean for her children.

Plan surveillance for motor neuron disease (weakness, wasting, fasciculations, dysphagia, dyspnoea) at each review, with EMG if lower motor neuron signs appear; the mildly brisk reflexes alone do not establish it.
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances (impulsive online spending), her teaching post, and lasting power of attorney while she can still take part.
Arrange caregiver education and support, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not part of the FTD work-up; FDG-PET, or perfusion SPECT where FDG-PET is unavailable, is the functional study when one is needed.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, familial, with ALS in a first-degree relative

For: anxiety history, maternal 'nervous breakdown'. Against: new progressive behavioural change at 55 with functional decline and frontal atrophy.

Mild bifrontal and anterior temporal atrophy with preserved posterior cortex on MRI, the imaging support probable bvFTD requires.
Free recall is disproportionately impaired with only borderline hippocampal volume, which keeps Alzheimer disease in the differential until a biomarker is obtained or the course clarifies it.
A brother with ALS at 60 and a mother with mid-life psychiatric illness suggest a C9orf72 FTD-ALS pedigree and support offering genetic counselling and testing.
Mildly brisk reflexes without weakness, wasting or fasciculations do not establish motor neuron disease.

clinical_assessment.impression: 4 of the 6 Rascovsky features are present on informant history and examination (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and perseverative or compulsive behaviour), with documented decline in daily function. This meets possible bvFTD; imaging and neuropsychological testing decide whether it is probable. Memory items are also impaired on the bedside screen (0/5 free recall, 3/5 with cues), which keeps Alzheimer disease in the differential.

Probable bvFTD requires functional decline and supportive imaging.
C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD.

Familial frontotemporal dementia and the.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD; counselling precedes any genetic test and any predictive testing of relatives. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R is a 57-year-old elementary school teacher currently on disability leave who presents to the cognitive neurology clinic with an 18-month history of progressive behavioral and personality changes, reported primarily by her adult daughter who accompanied her. Ms. R herself minimizes her difficulties and states that she 'just needs more rest.' Her daughter describes a woman who was formerly a dedicated and beloved teacher — organized, nurturing, and highly regarded in her community — who has undergone a profound transformation. Over the past 18 months, Ms. R has become increasingly impulsive, spending significant sums on online shopping without financial awareness or apparent concern. She has shown reduced empathy, repeatedly failing to acknowledge her daughter's distress during difficult life events and laughing at inappropriate times. She repeats the same short phrases and stories in conversation, often circling back to the same anecdote within minutes. She has been collecting cheap figurines in a compulsive fashion, filling her apartment with hundreds of identical items. She stopped attending her church, which she had done every Sunday for 35 years. Her grooming and hygiene have declined and her daughter must remind her to shower and change clothes. She was placed on disability leave 6 months ago after school parents and administrators raised concerns about her classroom behavior — she was reportedly making inappropriate personal comments to students and parents. Her episodic memory has also declined — she does not recall that her daughter was engaged until reminded, despite being told multiple times. Her brother died of ALS at age 60 six years ago. She is unaware of any genetic link between ALS and dementia.

neurological_exam.additional: Daughter reports the behavioral changes have been steadily progressive over 18 months. On bedside testing, free recall is severely impaired (0/5). Reflexes are mildly brisk (3+) at the knees and biceps without Babinski. Family history is notable for a brother who died of ALS.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No fasciculations of tongue. Gag reflex normal.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence. Mild stooped posture (chronic back pain). No parkinsonian shuffle.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Flat affect. MoCA 20/30: loses 3 points on executive tasks (trails, fluency: only 4 F-words in 1 minute), 5 on delayed recall (recalls 0/5 words at 5 minutes, recognizes 3/5 with cues), 1 on naming, 1 on attention. Memory is disproportionately impaired relative to the other domains. Clock drawing: completes but poor organization.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 throughout. No fasciculations, no rigidity, no tremor. Mild bilateral hyperreflexia (3+ patellar, 3+ biceps) — borderline, may be within normal variant.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 3+ patellar bilaterally, 3+ biceps bilaterally. No Babinski. No Hoffman. Palmomental reflex: bilateral positive.
